title: Verifier‑Grounded Generate‑Verify‑Repair for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Paired Mininet Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; 400 paired episodes) to evaluate whether a deterministic verifier‑grounded generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces operationally detectable policy‑violation errors when a hosted LLM produces device configuration sequences from operator intent in a Mininet emulation. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by both baseline and guarded). Baseline success (no detected policy violation) = 196/200 (98%); guarded success = 200/200 (100%). Paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.02; preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory test). An exploratory paired bootstrap (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) yields a 95% percentile CI = [0.005, 0.04]. Four verifier‑triggered repairs occurred (total hosted model calls = 204), giving mean extra model calls per intent = 0.02 and mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. All reported numeric values, provider‑call accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are drawn verbatim from the archived execution and analysis bundle. We interpret the preregistered confirmatory result conservatively and discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and operational implications.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation is a promising NetOps automation vector, but LLMs can produce mechanically detectable faults—syntax errors, topology/reachability violations, and ACL/policy mistakes—that may have operational consequences (availability loss, unintended access, or security exposure) [1], [4]. Closed‑loop generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipelines pair an LLM generator with a deterministic verifier that checks mechanizable constraints and, if violations occur, requests localized repairs from the model [2], [3]. Prior prototypes demonstrate utility of verifier‑grounded repair for mechanically checkable errors in code and domain‑specific program generation, yet open questions remain about scalability across heterogeneous vendor templates, concrete hosted‑LLM cost per avoided violation, and the interpretation of paired comparisons under shared_initial_candidate sampling semantics.

We preregistered study C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 to address these gaps with a confirmatory paired design executed in Mininet emulation. The design exercises three synthetic vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) and enforces shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled candidate per intent reused across baseline and guarded). The primary estimand compares the per‑intent probability of zero operationally detectable policy violations under guarded (GVR) versus baseline (single‑shot) generation using a predeclared exact McNemar two‑sided test. All artifacts, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis outputs are archived and referenced by the execution manifest; reported numeric values are taken verbatim from those artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Recent surveys and NetOps‑specific studies document rapid growth in LLM‑for‑NetOps research and recurring evaluation gaps: benchmark provenance, verifier integration, and limited multi‑vendor emulation evidence [5], [6]. Prototype NetOps experiments and adjacent domain work show LLMs can draft device configurations or configuration‑like artifacts but frequently introduce syntax/topology or policy errors; verifier‑guided repair recurs as an empirically supported mitigation pattern in code and domain program generation [2], [3]. NetConfEval and related benchmarks illustrate potential but remain task‑limited and often lack provenance‑traced verifier pipelines [4].

Our study builds directly on these lines by (i) applying a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory design across heterogeneous synthetic vendor templates in an emulator, (ii) executing and documenting shared_initial_candidate semantics so paired differences derive solely from deterministic validator/repair actions, and (iii) recording complete provider and verifier accounting to quantify repair cost in concrete hosted‑LLM call counts. We avoid claims of production readiness and position this work as an artifact‑grounded proof‑of‑concept evaluation under tightly specified scope.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered as C1‑GVR‑multivendor‑2026‑v1 prior to any model calls. The preregistration SHA‑256 is 9e0fc992665835975b01289f7841926ef6abf3584252c5d0459ba0ecf166bb50. The primary confirmatory estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (probability that an intent yields zero operationally detectable violations under guarded minus baseline) tested via exact McNemar two‑sided test (α = 0.05). Exploratory estimators (predeclared) include a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the risk difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and descriptive cost metrics (mean extra hosted model calls per intent and mean extra calls per avoided violation).

Sampling, strata, and shared_initial_candidate semantics: N = 200 unique operator intents were deterministically selected and stratified across three vendor‑template families and four topology patterns (12 strata) according to the frozen task_index_profile. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial sampled generation per intent was produced and reused by both baseline and guarded episodes. Under this semantics, for each intent the baseline outcome equals the validator verdict on that shared initial candidate; the guarded outcome equals the final guarded pipeline result after deterministic validation and any permitted repair. The preregistration explicitly declared that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; results therefore measure only validator/repair effects, not differences in first‑pass sampling or prompt templates.

Model configuration, temperature notation, and budget: The declared model in archived execution artifacts is gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; we state explicitly that null/unset is not evidence of deterministic provider sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Planned budget: planned_episode_count = 400, initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1, maximum_model_calls = 400.

Deterministic validator and repair policy: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements syntactic parsing, required‑command sequencing checks, reachability/topology verification against the emulated network state, and encoded ACL/policy checks derived from per‑task payload constraints. The validator issues a boolean success = "no detected violations" under the preregistered scoring rule full_intent_constraint_validation. The guarded pipeline allowed up to one verifier‑triggered repair call per intent; repair prompts were constructed from the validator's localized diagnostics to request corrective modifications. Repair calls were issued only when the validator reported violations. Validator traces (validation_before and validation_after) and repair decisions are archived per episode.

Scoring, missingness, and analysis plan: The primary analysis is exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary success indicators. The preregistration specified missingness and exclusion rules: pairs with deterministic duplicate detection or unrecoverable infrastructure failures would be excluded and reported; ambiguous validator outputs are conservatively treated as violations in the primary analysis. In execution no pairs were excluded and no episodes failed. The preregistered exploratory analyses included the paired bootstrap percentile CI (seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples) and descriptive cost accounting; bootstrap CI results are reported as exploratory and interpreted cautiously given potential instability with small discordant counts.

Deterministic accounting and provider audit: The execution_manifest records hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared_initial_generation events and 4 repair calls; cache_hit_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 204. Stage accounting reported shared_initial_generation = 200 and repair stage = 4. These audited counts are reported verbatim in Results to enable reproducibility reconciliation with archived artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and raw counts: The run completed per preregistration: planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; complete_pair_count = 200; failed_episode_count = 0. The analysis paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is: n11 = 196 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline succeed), n00 = 0 (both fail). Baseline success rate = 196/200 = 0.98; guarded success rate = 200/200 = 1.0; paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.02.

Confirmatory test and exploratory interval: The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on the paired binary outcomes yields p = 0.125 (primary confirmatory result; do not reject at α = 0.05). The archived exploratory paired bootstrap (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) produced a 95% percentile CI for the paired risk difference = [0.005, 0.04]. The bootstrap computation and seed are archived (analysis_log.jsonl) and reported here as descriptive context; the preregistered McNemar exact test remains the formal confirmatory inference. We add an explicit caution: when discordant pair counts (n10 + n01) are small, resampling intervals can be unstable and should be interpreted as exploratory magnitude indicators rather than confirmatory evidence.

Repair and cost accounting: Four verifier‑triggered repairs were invoked across the 200 intents (repair_calls = 4). Total hosted model calls = 204 (200 shared initial + 4 repairs), yielding mean hosted model calls per intent = 1.02 and mean extra calls per intent due to repairs = 0.02. Because each repair corrected one baseline failure in the archived contingency, mean extra calls per avoided violation = 1.0. These arithmetic derivations follow directly from the audited provider_call counts in the deterministic_reconciliation and execution_manifest artifacts.

Representative validator traces and example episodes: Representative execution/scoring task entries (execution/scoring/task-000004-*.json, task-000005-*, task-000006-*) show identical shared_initial_candidate content and identical baseline and guarded shared_initial responses (shared_initial text files reused by both conditions). For the corrected discordant pairs, validator_trace.validation_before recorded the detected violation and validator_trace.validation_after recorded that a repair was applied (repair_applied = true) and the final configuration passed full_intent_constraint_validation. These per‑episode artifacts substantiate the contingency table and repair accounting reported above.

Statistical diagnostics and power context: The preregistered power plan targeted detection of a 10 percentage point absolute reduction with N ≈ 157 (McNemar approximation), and N = 200 was chosen to permit stratified descriptions. The observed baseline failure prevalence (2%) was lower than some sensitivity scenarios used in planning, reducing power to detect small absolute improvements; this explains the non‑significant McNemar result despite a positive point estimate and is consistent with the small discordant count (4). We therefore treat the confirmatory p‑value as definitive for hypothesis testing and the bootstrap interval as supplemental magnitude information.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under shared_initial_candidate semantics: Because the experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled initial generation per intent reused by baseline and guarded), any paired improvement derives solely from deterministic validator/repair actions rather than from independent first‑pass re‑sampling or prompt changes. The preregistration explicitly stated that independent constrained‑prompt arms were not executed; readers should therefore not attribute guarded improvements to prompt engineering or to different initial generations.

Operational implications and bounded claims: Within the constrained Mininet emulation, synthetic vendor templates, and the validator's encoded rule set, a small repair budget (four repairs) removed the mechanically detectable baseline violations. The low absolute baseline failure prevalence (2%) implies modest repair activity sufficed for this workload. These artifact‑grounded results suggest that when a suitable deterministic verifier exists and provides localized, actionable feedback, bounded repair budgets can eliminate mechanically checkable faults in template‑driven emulated settings. We do not claim generalization to production hardware, other prompt families, different LLMs, or to semantic errors outside the validator's rule coverage.

Threats to validity: Construct validity—the deterministic validator covers syntactic, reachability/topology, and encoded ACL/policy checks, but cannot detect higher‑order semantic misinterpretations not expressible in its rules. Internal validity—the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed and verified in the deterministic_reconciliation; this prevents attributing observed gains to prompt engineering or independent re‑sampling. Conclusion validity—small discordant counts limit power and make resampling estimates less stable; the exact McNemar test is the appropriate confirmatory procedure under the preregistered design. External validity—single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic templates, and Mininet emulation limit claims about production readiness or multi‑model robustness.

Recommendations grounded in archived evidence: (1) Expand deterministic verifier coverage to formalize more semantic/policy ontologies and measure residual false negatives; (2) conduct paired designs with independent multi‑sample initial generations to isolate prompt/template effects (not executed here); (3) evaluate multiple hosted models and versions to assess robustness to provider nondeterminism; (4) preserve provenance tracing for all provider calls and validator traces to enable independent audit. Each recommendation follows directly from observed artifact evidence and stated limitations.

Reviewer‑requested clarifications addressed: We have (a) included explicit statements that temperature was null/unset and that null/unset does not imply temperature = 0; (b) clarified shared_initial_candidate semantics and their inferential consequences; (c) reported audited provider_call accounting verbatim (hosted_model_call_event_count = 204 decomposed as 200 shared initial + 4 repair calls) and explained how stage_counts map to the shared design; (d) added the bootstrap caution about small discordant counts; and (e) preserved the immutable master_prompt locator and SHA‑256 in the Disclosure Statement below, as required.
sections.conclusion:
We preregistered and executed a provenance‑traced paired confirmatory study (N = 200 intents; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to measure whether a deterministic verifier plus bounded repair reduces mechanically detectable policy violations for intent→configuration tasks in a Mininet emulation. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test did not reject at α = 0.05 (p = 0.125). Guarded GVR invoked four repairs and corrected the four observed baseline violations at low model‑call overhead (mean extra calls per intent = 0.02), yielding a paired risk difference estimate of 0.02 and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI = [0.005, 0.04] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). These artifact‑grounded results indicate that when a deterministic verifier can express and check relevant constraints and provide localized feedback, a small repair budget can eliminate mechanically detectable policy violations in similar template‑based emulated settings. The results do not establish production readiness, multi‑model generality, or coverage for semantic errors outside the validator. Future preregistered, provenance‑traced evaluations should expand verifier coverage, evaluate multiple hosted models, and compare independent multi‑sample baselines.

limitations: Scope limited to Mininet‑style emulation with synthetic, provenance‑traced intent→configuration tasks; results do not generalize directly to production hardware or live operations.
Single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) evaluated; multi‑model generality is not established.

Deterministic validator coverage limited to mechanically checkable errors (syntax, reachability, ACL/policy encodings); higher‑level semantic or specification misinterpretations outside the validator may remain undetected.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics imply observed paired differences derive only from verifier‑triggered repair; this design does not measure effects of alternative prompting strategies or independent multi‑sample candidate selection.

Observed confirmatory effect (2 percentage points) did not reach statistical significance at α = 0.05 for N = 200 (exact McNemar p = 0.125); low baseline failure prevalence (2%) reduced power to detect small absolute improvements under some preregistered scenarios.
